## Learning outcomes

By the end of this part, you should be able to:

- Direct `Claude Code` to scaffold and extend a `Next.js` app of your own choosing across multiple sessions
- Practise the sprint's context habit: an `AGENTS.md` kept up to date with your app's details and rules
- Run and verify a `Next.js` app locally in your browser

<br>

---

<br>

## Overview

In this Sprint 1 project, practise directing `Claude Code` with a clear brief and managing context with `AGENTS.md`.

| Area | Guideline | Details |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **What to build** | Build a small `Next.js` app of your own | **Choose something you want to build.** If nothing comes to mind, there is a document-app sketch further down you can build instead. |
| **Scope & polish** | Practise the workflow, not perfection | Keep it small and do not try to perfect it. Later sprints add databases, user accounts, and deployment, so anything you leave rough now will have better tools soon. |
| **Environment** | Local only (`localhost:3000`) | The project is not deployed to the public internet. Everything (building, testing, and submitting) happens on your own machine. |

<br>

<br>

## Task description

You are building a small `Next.js` app of your own choosing. It might be a recipe box, a workout log, a reading list, a link saver, or the document app sketched below. What the app *is* is up to you. How you build it, and the framework you build it with, are fixed.

The stack stays the same whatever you build:

- `Next.js` (App Router)
- `TypeScript`
- `Tailwind CSS`

The project also has these constraints:

- The app runs locally via `npm run dev` (the command that starts your app on your machine) and you check it at `localhost:3000`.
- There is no deployment step and no public URL.
- There is no backend and no user accounts.
- **Data persists through a browser mechanism you decide on with `Claude Code`** (see *Approach to solving the task* below).

Everything else is your call: what the app does, how it looks, what features it has beyond the must-haves.

Use the sprint's techniques to direct the agent to build your app.

<br>

---

<br>

## Requirements

Your app must have the capabilities below. **Adapt each one to your chosen app**, and keep the scope small.

- [ ] At least two pages, including one detail page with its own web address (for example `/items/abc123`) that opens the right item directly.
- [ ] The user can create, edit, and delete the main thing your app is about.
- [ ] Use `Claude Code` to research browser storage options, choose a mechanism that fits your single-user, no-backend app, and implement it. Check that created items, edits, and deletions are saved after a full page reload and after closing and reopening the tab.
- [ ] No blank screens: a readable message when there is nothing yet, and a friendly "not found" message for an address that does not exist.
- [ ] A usable, responsive layout that works on a laptop and on a phone.

Add other features only if you have time.

## Need an idea? The document app

You can build the document app if you need an idea. It is a personal writing workspace in your browser, and the sketch below is **one way to build it, not a checklist to satisfy.**

One way to shape it:

- A two-pane workspace: a list of documents down one side, an editing area on the other.

<img src="https://intra-content-image-bucket.s3.eu-north-1.amazonaws.com/images/bc8c3b08-aec0-46f5-8d1b-0466711772fe.png" width="800" alt="Two-pane document workspace layout" />

- The user can create a new document, edit its title and body, and delete it.
- A search box in the list that filters documents by title as the user types.
- Documents that are still there when the page is reloaded.
- Each document at its own web address, so a bookmark opens it directly in the same browser where it was saved.
- Basic Markdown formatting in the body (headings, bold, italic, bullet lists), with a way to switch between editing and a formatted preview.

<img src="https://intra-content-image-bucket.s3.eu-north-1.amazonaws.com/images/e0941581-e447-4651-8bd2-22ad712b3517.png" width="800" alt="Markdown editor with edit and preview modes" />

- A layout that stays usable from laptop width down to phone width.

<img src="https://intra-content-image-bucket.s3.eu-north-1.amazonaws.com/images/060895a3-373d-4724-825e-811bb52104d7.png" width="800" alt="Desktop and mobile responsive layouts of the document app" />

<br>

### Other ideas

Any small, single-focus app works. Here are a few ideas:

- **Recipe box:** save recipes, open each at its own address, search by name.
- **Workout log:** log sessions, edit and delete them, and still see them after a reload.
- **Link saver:** paste a link with a note, tag it, and open each saved item's page.
- **Reading list:** add books, mark them read, and filter the list.

## Additional ideas (optional)

These are **ideas, not requirements.** If your must-haves work and you want to practise directing the agent through a feature that was not in the original scaffold, pick one. Or invent your own.

- **Starred or pinned items.** A star button pins favourites to the top of the list, and the starred state survives a reload.
- **Dark-mode toggle.** A switch flips the app between light and dark themes, and the choice sticks across reloads.
- **Tags.** Add tags to each item, show them in the list, and let the user filter by tag.
- **Export / import.** A button that downloads everything as a file, and a picker that reads it back in.
- **Live count or stats.** A running total somewhere useful, such as a word count or an item count.

Add one only if you have time.

## Recommendations

These are **recommendations, not pass/fail criteria.** You will discuss the ones you used in your review.

- **An up-to-date `AGENTS.md`.** After every few features, have the agent add what the app is, how to run it, and one or two plain-language rules (for example, *"use the App Router, not the Pages Router"* or *"do not add new libraries without asking first"*).
- **A sensible `.gitignore`.** Keep `node_modules/`, `.env`, and OS or editor clutter out of the repo, the same habit you rehearsed in the practice project.
- **Work on app design.** Give the agent specific visual direction for the app.

> **Reflection:** You will not be graded on ticking every recommendation off. You will be asked to talk about the ones you used and what they changed.

## Evaluation criteria

Open the app at `localhost:3000` for the review.

The review centres on three things:

- **A working `Next.js` app of your own choosing** that meets the must-have capabilities and runs locally at `localhost:3000`.
- **Evidence you directed the agent using the sprint's techniques**, such as how you used `AGENTS.md` to guide it.
- **Persistence research and implementation:** explain the options you researched with `Claude Code`, why you chose your browser storage mechanism, and demonstrate that creations, edits, and deletions remain saved after reloading and reopening the tab.

> **Note:** A small, unpolished app passes if it meets the must-have capabilities. You do not need a finished product or a stretch feature.

## Approach to solving the task

<img src="https://intra-content-image-bucket.s3.eu-north-1.amazonaws.com/images/3c5c812b-011e-4f8c-953b-75191ce463bc.png" width="600" alt="Next.js App Router getting started documentation" />

*To get a better understanding of `Next.js`, go to [nextjs.org/docs](https://nextjs.org/docs) and skim the topics that interest you.*

**Decide what to build and scope it down first.** Write one or two sentences describing your app and the single thing it should do well. If it needs more than a handful of screens, it is too big. Trim it, or build the document app sketched above.

`Next.js` 16.3 and later create agent instructions when scaffolding a new project or when the development server detects a coding agent. Its generated block points the agent at documentation matching your `Next.js` version. At the start of each session, check that `Claude Code` has loaded `AGENTS.md`, or ask it to read and follow the file. After every few updates, ask `Claude Code` to update `AGENTS.md` with what the app does, its pages, how data is saved, how to run it, and any rules you have settled on, such as "do not add new libraries without asking first". Keep the generated `Next.js` block intact; your notes go alongside it.

```text
Add what has changed in my app since the last update to AGENTS.md: what it
does now, the pages it has, how its data is saved, and how to run it. Leave
the Next.js block as it is.
```

Persistence research and implementation are required. Before building features, ask `Claude Code` to research how to keep your app's data in the browser. Describe your app in plain language:

```text
I'm building a small single-user app that runs locally on my own machine.
There's no backend, database, or login. Created items, edits, and deletions
need to stay saved after reloading the page and closing and reopening the
tab. Research the browser storage options and show me the sources you use.
Explain the trade-offs and recommend an option that fits my app before
changing anything.
```

Choose a mechanism based on the research, then ask `Claude Code` to implement it in your app. Test creating, editing, and deleting items, then reload the page and close and reopen the tab to check that each change stays saved. In your review, demonstrate persistence and explain your choice, why it fits, and the alternatives you considered.

Build one feature at a time and commit at every stable state:

1. Basic shell and pages
2. Creating, editing, and deleting your main item, with persistence
3. Search and empty states
4. Responsive layout and formatting
5. An optional stretch feature

Never ask the agent to build the whole app in a single prompt.

If time allows, take 30 to 60 minutes for a design pass once the must-haves work. Give `Claude Code` specific direction rather than a vague "make it nicer": pick a tone (clean and minimal, dense, playful, editorial) and specify typography, spacing, colours, and button shape. Review the changes in your browser.

If a session breaks the app, reset to the last good commit.

## Submission

Read an [in-depth guide about reviews here](https://doku.turingcollege.com/p/0771306d-bc1e-4b00-9153-c63adeb63a85).

#### Submission and scheduling a project review

Submit through the `GitHub` repository created for you so the reviewer can see your work beforehand. These materials explain how to submit, schedule a review, and use `GitHub`:

- [Completing a Sprint, Submitting a Project and Scheduling Reviews](https://doku-v02-production.up.railway.app/p/f3dbf8bc-2dae-4230-938d-3144110ea74a)
- [Git and GitHub for Beginners](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RGOj5yH7evk)

Hand in the following before your 1-1 review call:

- **Your Turing College `GitHub` repository URL.**
- **`README.md`** covering: what you built, how to run it locally, and a screenshot of the app.

Include this too if you updated it:

- **`AGENTS.md`** at the repo root, updated with your app's details and the rules the agent was asked to follow.

In your review call, be ready to talk through:

1. What you chose to build and how you scoped it down.
2. How you researched and implemented persistence with `Claude Code`: which browser storage mechanism you chose, why it fits a single-user, no-backend app, and what alternatives you considered. Demonstrate that creations, edits, and deletions stay saved after reloading and reopening the tab.
3. One moment a Sprint 1 technique changed the outcome, such as `AGENTS.md` catching the agent drifting.
4. The design pass, if you did one: the direction you gave and what changed from the scaffolded default.
5. One thing that was harder than the plain-`HTML` app from the static-site lesson.
6. What you would keep or change next time.
